1#main: The forms of an open parashah and a closed parashah, and the form of song. In it are 6 seifim. A parashah that he made closed, or a closed one that he made open—he should put away (genizah). {Rama: And some say it is permitted to correct it like other errors (Rosh, Rashba, and Rivash); and so scribes are accustomed to correct it if he can erase without harming a Name, for he may not cut out the Name and make holes in the sheet (Rosh, general rule 3).}
2#main: Regarding the form of open and closed there is a dispute between the Rambam and the Rosh; and one who fears Heaven should satisfy all of them and do as follows: for an open parashah he finishes the preceding parashah in the middle of a line and leaves at its end a space of nine letters, and begins to write at the head of the line beneath it; and for a closed parashah he always finishes the preceding parashah at the beginning of a line, leaves a space of nine letters, and begins to write at the end of that same line. And he should not change to make another form, neither for open nor for closed—and thus it is valid both for the Rambam and for the Rosh. {Rama: And if he cannot aim thus, he should not deviate from the Rambam's words, for the Acharonim relied on him and wrote that his words are primary (Mordechai in the name of a certain sage). Nevertheless, if a Sefer Torah is found not written according to his words, one does not declare it invalid, for there are great authorities with other views in this (R' Yitzchak Minz siman 8).}
3#main: If he wrote the song like the rest of the writing, or wrote the rest of the writing like the song—it is invalid. And specifically when he wrote the song like ordinary writing without dispersion; but if he changed the dispersion from what is customary, he does not invalidate it, provided it be "a brick upon a brick" (°).
4#main: The Song at the Sea—one writes it in thirty-two lines: the first line in the usual manner, and for the other lines one leaves one space in the middle, and one leaves space in two places in the middle until the line is divided into three, and space is found opposite the writing and writing opposite the space.
5#main: The form of the Song of Haazinu: each line has one space in the middle, and each line is found divided into two; and one writes it in seventy lines.
6#main: If he wrote plene what should be defective, or defective what should be plene; or wrote a word that is kri ukhetiv according to its kri, such as writing "yishkavenah" instead of "yishgalenah," or "uvetachorim" instead of "uvecholilim," and the like—it is invalid. {Rama: And there are other matters scribes are accustomed in, transmitted person to person, such as large and small letters, points, and crowns. And they are also accustomed regarding the count of lines to make them not fewer than forty-two, and some say forty-eight, and not more than sixty. And they are accustomed at the heads of lines above the Song at the Sea five lines, and these are their beginnings: haba'im, bayabashah, ham, met, bemitzrayim. And likewise below the song five lines, and their beginnings: vetikach, sus, vayetze'u, vayavo'u. And above the Song of Haazinu six lines, and their beginnings: ve'aidah, achari, haderech, be'acharit, lehach'iso, kehal. And below, five lines, and their beginnings: vayavo, vayedaber, asher, hazot, [asher]. And all these matters are for the mitzvah; and if one changed, he does not invalidate (all from the language of the Tur).}
